title: 09. Evaluation: Golden Datasets: The Foundation of Trustworthy AI Evaluation

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: > **Prerequisite**: Files 01–09. You understand how to score LLM, RAG, agent, and tool-calling outputs; you understand tracing and monitoring. This file is about the *ground truth* those scores are scored against. Without a golden dataset, every metric in this guide is a vibe.

sections.title: 1. What is a Golden Dataset?
sections.body:
A **golden dataset** is a curated, labeled set of inputs and their expected outputs that serves as the ground truth for evaluating an AI system. "Golden" because it is the standard against which every model, prompt, and retrieval change is measured — the reference meter stick.

A golden example has four required components:

- **Input** — the prompt, query, or conversation the system must handle.
- **Expected output** — the correct answer, the right tool call, the relevant retrieved docs, or an explicit rubric for what counts as correct.
- **Metadata** — category, difficulty, language, user segment, source.
- **Scoring rubric** — how to grade a model output against the expected output (exact match? semantic match? partial credit?).

Two distinctions matter:

- **Golden dataset vs training data.** Training data teaches the model parameters; the golden dataset measures the model. If your golden set ever leaks into fine-tuning data, your eval scores become meaningless — you're grading the model on what it memorized.
- **Golden dataset vs benchmark.** A benchmark (MMLU, HumanEval, GAIA) is a public, general-purpose yardstick. A golden dataset is *yours*: it reflects your users, your domain, your failure modes. Benchmarks tell you how you compare to the field; golden sets tell you whether you regressed on your own users.

```
                    ┌─────────────────────────┐
   new model/prompt │  Golden Dataset         │
      ─────────────>│  inputs + expected      │
                    │  outputs + rubrics      │
                    └───────────┬─────────────┘
                                │ run model on each input
                                v
                    ┌─────────────────────────┐
                    │  Model outputs          │
                    └───────────┬─────────────┘
                                │ compare vs expected, apply rubric
                                v
                    ┌─────────────────────────┐
                    │  Scorer (rule /         │
                    │  LLM-as-judge)          │
                    └───────────┬─────────────┘
                                │
                                v
                    ┌─────────────────────────┐
                    │  Metrics + slicing      │
                    │  pass / fail / regress  │
                    └─────────────────────────┘
```

sections.title: 2. Why You Need a Golden Dataset
sections.body:
Without a golden set you are flying blind. Every change to a prompt, a retrieval threshold, or a model version becomes a debate about *vibes*: "I tried it on five queries and it felt better." Five queries chosen how? Better on which segment? Felt by whom? Without ground truth, "better" is unfalsifiable.

**Real story.** A team shipped a prompt rewrite for their support bot. It read cleaner in code review, scored higher on their ad-hoc vibe checks, and was deployed. Two weeks later, ticket deflection dropped 11%. The new prompt subtly broke refund-policy questions — it would advise a "5-7 business day" refund window for a tier of customers whose contract guaranteed 48 hours. The team had no golden set, no regression test, no pre-deploy gate. They discovered the regression in a quarterly business review, weeks after the damage. The fix took 20 minutes; the lost trust took quarters.

With a golden set, the same change would have failed pre-deploy gating: the refund-policy examples in the set would have flagged the wrong window before the prompt ever touched production.

Golden datasets enable four core workflows:

- **Pre-deployment gating** — a new model/prompt must not regress on the golden set before shipping.
- **Continuous regression testing** — run the golden set nightly against the live model; alert on any metric drop.
- **Fair comparison across versions** — model A vs model B vs prompt v1 vs v2, all on the same examples.
- **Calibration of LLM-as-judge** — the judge is validated against the golden set's human labels; without that calibration, judge scores are just another opinion.

sections.title: 3. Anatomy of a Good Golden Dataset
sections.body:
Every example should carry enough structure to be scored, sliced, and audited years later. A minimal schema:

| Field | Type | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | string | `q-0421` | Unique, never reused, never deleted (deprecate instead) |
| `input` | object | `{"prompt": "...", "context": [...]}` | Prompt + any retrieved context or system state |
| `expected` | object | `{"answer": "...", "tool_calls": [...]}` | Ground truth answer, trajectory, or expected retrieved docs |
| `category` | string | `billing` | For slicing and coverage analysis |
| `difficulty` | enum | `hard` | easy / medium / hard |
| `language` | string | `en-US` | Locale; matters for multilingual systems |
| `user_segment` | string | `enterprise` | Who this query represents |
| `source` | enum | `production` | production / expert / synthetic |
| `rubric` | string | `"exact match + tone"` | How to grade the model's output |
| `version` | string | `1.3.0` | Dataset version when this example was added |
| `added_at` | ISO date | `2025-03-14` | Provenance |
| `notes` | string | `"Edge: non-US currency"` | Free-form context for future maintainers |

The two fields teams most often skip are `rubric` and `source`. Skip `rubric` and every scorer has to re-invent what "correct" means; skip `source` and you can't tell, six months later, whether an example came from a real user or from a GPT-4 brainstorm — which matters a lot when you discover it's wrong.

sections.title: 4. How to Build a Golden Dataset
sections.body:
Three sources, in descending order of value.

### A. From Production Traffic (best)

Real user queries are the gold standard because they reflect the actual distribution of what your system must handle. The pipeline is: sample → filter → annotate.

- **Sample** production logs (with PII redaction).
- **Filter**: deduplicate near-identical queries, remove PII, balance across categories (don't let "password reset" dominate because it's the most common query).
- **Annotate** each filtered query with ground truth (human, LLM-assisted, or hybrid — see Section 6).

```python
import json, random
from collections import Counter

def sample_production(log_path, k=200, seed=42):
    """Sample k diverse production queries for golden-set annotation."""
    random.seed(seed)
    queries = [json.loads(line) for line in open(log_path)]
    seen, uniq = set(), []
    for q in queries:                                  # 1. dedup on normalized text
        key = " ".join(q["prompt"].lower().split())
        if key not in seen:
            seen.add(key); uniq.append(q)
    by_cat = {}                                        # 2. stratified by category
    for q in uniq:
        by_cat.setdefault(q["category"], []).append(q)
    per_cat = max(1, k // max(1, len(by_cat)))
    sampled = []
    for items in by_cat.values():
        random.shuffle(items); sampled.extend(items[:per_cat])
    return sampled
```

### B. From Experts / SMEs

Hand-crafted by domain experts for edge cases production traffic won't surface often enough: rare refund-policy corners, regulated industries, multilingual edge cases, multi-step reasoning chains that real users rarely articulate cleanly. Expensive — $20–$200 per example once you count SME time — but irreplaceable for coverage of the long tail. Best used to fill specific gaps in production-sourced data.

### C. From Synthetic Generation

Use a strong LLM (GPT-4-class or larger) to generate diverse queries and expected answers for a given topic. Cheap and fast. Two risks: the LLM's query distribution drifts toward LLM-flavored phrasing (not how real users talk), and the LLM can produce subtly wrong expected answers that look plausible. Best for bootstrapping a new category or filling coverage gaps before production traffic accumulates.

```python
SYNTH_GEN_PROMPT = """You are generating diverse user queries for an internal
IT-support chatbot.

Topic: {topic}
Constraints:
- Vary phrasing, formality, and specificity.
- Include 2 easy, 3 medium, and 1 hard query.
- Avoid queries already in this list: {existing}
- Each query on its own line, prefixed with [easy]/[medium]/[hard].

Return 6 queries. No commentary."""
```

A pragmatic build order: start with 30% production + 70% synthetic to bootstrap coverage, then shift toward 70% production + 20% expert + 10% synthetic as traffic accumulates.

sections.title: 5. Sizing Your Golden Dataset
sections.body:
Too small and your metrics are noisy — a single example flipping from pass to fail moves your score by 5%. Too large and annotation cost balloons, eval runtime grows, and maintenance becomes a chore. The right size depends on the smallest regression you want to detect.

**Rule of thumb:**

- **Binary tasks** (pass/fail, correct/incorrect): 100–300 examples.
- **Graded tasks** (0–5 rubric): 500–1000 examples.
- **Fine-grained / multi-criteria** (RAG faithfulness + relevance + citation accuracy): 1000+.

These numbers come from statistical power. For a binomial pass rate at alpha=0.05 and power=0.8, the smallest detectable absolute effect at common sample sizes:

```
   n (examples)  |  smallest detectable absolute regression
   ------------- |  -----------------------------------------
        50       |    ~14%       (e.g., 85%  vs  71%)
       100       |    ~10%
       300       |    ~6%
      1000       |    ~3%
      3000       |    ~2%
   ------------- |  -----------------------------------------
```

If your team ships changes that move the needle by ~5% and your golden set has 50 examples, you will *not* detect the regression — it'll be invisible in the noise. Either grow the set or accept that 5%-scale regressions are below your detection floor.

**Stratified sampling** matters as much as total size. 300 examples all from the "account" category tell you nothing about "billing" regressions. Stratify by category, difficulty, language, and user segment; track per-stratum counts and ensure each stratum has enough examples (~30 minimum) to detect its own regressions.

sections.title: 6. Annotation Strategy
sections.body:
Ground truth has to be *true*, which makes annotation the hardest part of building a golden set.

### Human annotation

Three pillars:

- **Annotator guidelines** — a written document defining what "correct" means, with worked examples for each judgment call. Without guidelines, every annotator applies their own definition and your labels are noise.
- **Inter-annotator agreement (IAA)** — have multiple annotators label the same subset and measure agreement. **Cohen's kappa** for two annotators, **Krippendorff's alpha** for many. Target kappa > 0.7; below 0.4 means your labels are barely better than chance.
- **Adjudication** — disagreements go to a senior annotator or SME for a final ruling. Log the disagreement and the resolution; over time, patterns in disagreements reveal ambiguities in your guidelines.

### LLM-assisted annotation

Use a GPT-4-class model to propose labels, then have humans review. Sample 20% of LLM labels for human verification; if disagreement rate exceeds 10%, either improve the labeling prompt or fall back to full human annotation for that category. **Active learning** focuses human effort on cases the LLM is least confident about — high-value, low-cost.

### Hybrid: LLM proposes, human verifies

The dominant pattern in practice. The LLM does the bulk labeling at $0.01–$0.05 per example; humans verify a sample and label every uncertain case. Cost is 5–10x lower than full human annotation, with quality close to pure-human when the verification loop is honest.

sections.title: 7. Quality Control
sections.body:
A golden dataset is only trustworthy if it has been audited. Six checks:

- **Coverage check** — does the dataset cover every important scenario? Map categories against a taxonomy of user intents; gaps are bugs.
- **Difficulty distribution** — easy/medium/hard mix. A set that's 90% easy will look great on paper and miss every real failure mode.
- **Bias check** — demographic, topical, linguistic. If 80% of queries come from one user segment, your eval measures performance for that segment, not for all users.
- **Leakage check** — search the training/fine-tuning corpus for any golden example (verbatim or near-match). Leaked examples must be removed from eval, not just flagged.
- **Staleness check** — when was each example last reviewed? Examples older than 6–12 months should be re-validated; product reality drifts.
- **Adversarial subset** — deliberately hard cases: ambiguous queries, multi-step reasoning, prompt-injection attempts, multi-lingual code-switching. Track this subset separately so a model can't quietly regress on hard cases while keeping the easy average up.

sections.title: 8. Dataset Versioning & Maintenance
sections.body:
Golden datasets are living artifacts. They evolve as your product, users, and models evolve.

**Version with semver-like tags:**

- `MAJOR` (e.g., `1.0.0` → `2.0.0`): schema change or large rewrite; old scores not comparable.
- `MINOR` (e.g., `1.0.0` → `1.1.0`): examples added or removed; scores roughly comparable but per-stratum counts shift.
- `PATCH` (e.g., `1.0.0` → `1.0.1`): rubric clarified, typos fixed, metadata corrected; scores directly comparable.

Track every change: which examples were added, removed, or modified, by whom, and why. Old versions stay available for backward compatibility — last quarter's eval results must remain reproducible.

**Refresh cadence**: monthly for fast-moving products, quarterly for stable ones. Refresh when any of these fire:

- A new use case or feature shipped (new categories to cover).
- Distribution shift detected in production traffic (new query patterns the golden set doesn't represent).
- New failure modes discovered post-deploy (those failures belong in the golden set now).
- Model upgraded significantly (the failure-mode distribution will shift; old adversarial cases may be solved, new ones emerge).

sections.title: 9. The Golden Dataset → Eval → Production Loop
sections.body:
A golden dataset is the hub of a closed feedback loop that connects production failures to pre-deploy gating.

```
   ┌─────────────── prod traffic surfaces new failure modes ─────────────┐
   │                                                                     │
   v                                                                     │
 ┌──────────────────┐                          ┌──────────────────────┐  │
 │   Production     │  add failing cases as    │   Golden Dataset     │  │
 │   (real users)   │ ───────────────────────> │   (versioned)        │  │
 └──────────────────┘                          └──────────┬───────────┘  │
        ^                                                 │              │
        │ ship gated version                              │ run new      │
        │                                                 │ model/prompt │
        │                                                 v  on golden   │
 ┌──────────────────┐                          ┌──────────────────────┐  │
 │   Deploy         │ <─────────────────────── │   Eval               │  │
 │   (after pass)   │   gate / A/B / regress   │   (metrics + slices) │  │
 └──────────────────┘                          └──────────────────────┘  │
        │                                                                │
        └──────── new failures discovered post-deploy ───────────────────┘
                              (loop restarts)
```

The loop has four moves:

1. **Production → Golden**: real-user failures (from monitoring, support tickets, user feedback) become new golden examples.
2. **Golden → Eval**: every candidate model/prompt runs against the golden set; regressions block deploy.
3. **Eval → Deploy**: passing the golden gate is a precondition for production rollout.
4. **Deploy → Production**: post-deploy monitoring surfaces the *next* round of failures, restarting the loop.

This loop is what separates teams that improve over time from teams that ship regressions on a recurring basis. Without it, every failure is novel; with it, every failure is a one-time tax that buys permanent protection.

sections.title: 10. Tools for Golden Dataset Management
sections.body:
| Tool | Type | Strengths |
|------|------|-----------|
| Argilla | OSS | Annotation + dataset management; tight HF integration; active-learning hooks |
| Label Studio | OSS | General-purpose labeling; flexible schema; multi-modal |
| Cleanlab | Commercial | Auto-finds label errors and noisy examples in existing datasets |
| Hugging Face Datasets | OSS | Storage + versioning; de-facto interchange format |
| LangSmith Datasets | Commercial | Tight LangChain integration; trace → dataset extraction |
| Phoenix Datasets | OSS | Eval-focused; OpenInference-native; Arize-backed |
| DVC | OSS | Data versioning alongside code; reproducible ML pipelines |

A typical stack: DVC for versioning the raw files, Hugging Face Datasets as the interchange format, Argilla or Label Studio for human annotation, and an eval platform (LangSmith / Phoenix / Langfuse) for running the set against the model and slicing results.

sections.title: 11. Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
1. **Too small to be statistically meaningful.** 30 examples can't detect a 5% regression; you're measuring noise.
2. **No diversity.** All easy questions, one category, one language. Score looks great; production breaks.
3. **No adversarial examples.** The golden set measures the model on the easy 80%, not the hard 20% where it actually fails.
4. **Never refreshed.** A 12-month-old golden set drifts from production reality; new query patterns aren't represented, stale ones dominate.
5. **Treated as a static artifact.** A golden set is a living document. Owners, review cadence, and changelog are required.
6. **No annotation guidelines.** Without a written rubric, IAA collapses; labels are annotator-opinion noise.
7. **Leaked into training set.** Fine-tuning on data that includes golden examples makes eval scores meaningless. Always check.
8. **Biased toward one user segment.** If the golden set is built from one persona, your eval measures that persona's experience and silently under-serves the others.

sections.title: 12. Code Example
sections.body:
Minimal `GoldenDataset` class — `add`, `save`, `load`, `stats`, with coverage breakdown and near-duplicate detection. Pure Python, stdlib only. Save as `golden_dataset.py` and run.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""golden_dataset.py - Minimal GoldenDataset class for AI evaluation."""
from __future__ import annotations
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

@dataclass
class GoldenExample:
    id: str
    input: str
    expected: str
    category: str
    difficulty: str          # easy / medium / hard
    source: str              # production / expert / synthetic
    rubric: str              # how to grade
    version: str = "1.0.0"
    meta: dict = field(default_factory=dict)

class GoldenDataset:
    def __init__(self, name: str, version: str = "1.0.0"):
        self.name, self.version, self.examples = name, version, []

    def add(self, ex: GoldenExample) -> None:
        if any(e.id == ex.id for e in self.examples):
            raise ValueError(f"duplicate id: {ex.id}")
        self.examples.append(ex)

    def save(self, path: str) -> None:
        Path(path).write_text(json.dumps({
            "name": self.name, "version": self.version,
            "n": len(self.examples),
            "examples": [asdict(e) for e in self.examples]}, indent=2))

    @classmethod
    def load(cls, path: str) -> "GoldenDataset":
        p = json.loads(Path(path).read_text())
        ds = cls(name=p["name"], version=p["version"])
        for e in p["examples"]: ds.add(GoldenExample(**e))
        return ds

    def coverage(self) -> dict[str, dict[str, dict[str, float]]]:
        n = len(self.examples) or 1
        out = {}
        for axis in ("category", "difficulty", "source"):
            c = Counter(getattr(e, axis) for e in self.examples)
            out[axis] = {k: {"count": v, "frac": round(v / n, 3)} for k, v in c.items()}
        return out

    def find_duplicates(self, threshold: float = 0.8) -> list[tuple[str, str, float]]:
        def norm(s): return set(s.lower().split())
        dups = []
        for i, a in enumerate(self.examples):
            ta = norm(a.input)
            for j in range(i + 1, len(self.examples)):
                tb = norm(self.examples[j].input)
                union = len(ta | tb) or 1
                jacc = len(ta & tb) / union
                if jacc >= threshold:
                    dups.append((a.id, self.examples[j].id, round(jacc, 3)))
        return dups

    def stats(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {"name": self.name, "version": self.version,
                "n_examples": len(self.examples),
                "coverage": self.coverage(),
                "duplicates": self.find_duplicates()}

def build_demo_dataset() -> GoldenDataset:
    ds = GoldenDataset("support-bot-golden", version="1.2.0")
    rows = [
        ("q-001", "How do I reset my password?",
         "Send reset link via email; expires in 15 min.", "account", "easy",
         "production", "Exact-answer match + tone"),
        ("q-002", "Reset password not received",
         "Verify email; resend link; check spam.", "account", "medium",
         "production", "Step-completion + empathy"),
        ("q-003", "How do I cancel my subscription?",
         "Settings > Billing > Cancel; refund prorated.", "billing", "easy",
         "production", "Exact-answer match"),
        ("q-004", "Refund for cancelled order",
         "Refund if within 30 days; 5-7 business days.", "billing", "medium",
         "expert", "Step-completion + policy accuracy"),
        ("q-005", "App crashes on startup on Android 14",
         "Clear cache; reinstall; escalate if persists.", "technical", "hard",
         "expert", "Diagnostic steps + escalation"),
        ("q-006", "Does the app support offline mode?",
         "Yes, read-only; cached docs available offline.", "technical", "easy",
         "production", "Exact-answer match"),
        ("q-007", "How do I export my data to CSV?",
         "Settings > Privacy > Export; email within 24h.", "account", "medium",
         "production", "Step-completion"),
        ("q-008", "Reset password not received",
         "Verify email; resend link; check spam folder.", "account", "medium",
         "synthetic", "Step-completion + empathy"),  # near-dup of q-002
    ]
    for r in rows:
        ds.add(GoldenExample(id=r[0], input=r[1], expected=r[2], category=r[3],
                             difficulty=r[4], source=r[5], rubric=r[6]))
    return ds

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ds = build_demo_dataset()
    print(f"=== {ds.name} v{ds.version} ===  ({len(ds.examples)} examples)")
    print("\n--- Coverage ---")
    for axis, buckets in ds.coverage().items():
        print(f"{axis}:")
        for k, v in sorted(buckets.items()):
            print(f"  {k:10s} -> n={v['count']}  ({v['frac']*100:.1f}%)")
    print("\n--- Duplicate detection ---")
    for a, b, j in ds.find_duplicates():
        print(f"  NEAR-DUP: {a} <-> {b}  (jaccard={j})")
    ds.save("/tmp/golden_demo.json")
    print(f"\nSaved /tmp/golden_demo.json; "
          f"reloaded {len(GoldenDataset.load('/tmp/golden_demo.json').examples)} examples")
```

**Expected output:**

```
=== support-bot-golden v1.2.0 ===  (8 examples)

--- Coverage ---
category:
  account    -> n=4  (50.0%)
  billing    -> n=2  (25.0%)
  technical  -> n=2  (25.0%)
difficulty:
  easy       -> n=3  (37.5%)
  hard       -> n=1  (12.5%)
  medium     -> n=4  (50.0%)
source:
  expert     -> n=2  (25.0%)
  production -> n=5  (62.5%)
  synthetic  -> n=1  (12.5%)

--- Duplicate detection ---
  NEAR-DUP: q-002 <-> q-008  (jaccard=1.0)

Saved /tmp/golden_demo.json; reloaded 8 examples
```

The duplicate detector catches that `q-008` (synthetic) is identical to `q-002` (production) — a real issue when synthetic generators fill coverage gaps without deduping against existing examples.

quiz.explanation: Monthly for fast-moving products, quarterly for stable ones — but also event-driven: ship a new feature, detect production distribution shift, discover a new failure mode, or upgrade the model significantly. A stale golden set measures performance against last year's users, which is worse than no eval because it gives false confidence.

quiz.question: What is dataset leakage, and why is it fatal?
options: Random sampling over-represents common categories (password reset) and under-represents rare but important ones (refund disputes, regulated industries).

quiz.explanation: Leakage is when golden examples appear (verbatim or near-match) in the training or fine-tuning corpus. The model memorizes them, scores perfectly on eval, and fails on everything else. Always grep the training data for golden inputs before each eval run; use near-duplicate detection, not just exact match, because paraphrased leaks are just as damaging.
